summary.text: Dog 1, an intact male German Shepherd aged 0.5 years and weighing 5.0 kg, had idiopathic paraphimosis with signs lasting 1 month. Examination upon presentation showed permanent penile protrusion, and the penile protrusion measured 2.0 cm. The prepuce could easily be moved cranially to cover the protruded penis.

The dog underwent modified preputial elevation and cranial translation of the prepuce, with 4.0 cm of preputial translation, under general isoflurane anaesthesia. After surgery it was hospitalised for 2 days and received cryotherapy with ice packs. Re-examination 5 and 14 days after surgery found it clinically healthy with no signs of paraphimosis. No orchiectomy was performed at the time of surgery.

A small amount of serosanguineous discharge from the cranial incision resolved within 24 hours without intervention. No long-term complications were recorded. Follow-up lasted 36 months with an excellent outcome.

summary.text: Dog 2, an intact male mixed breed aged 4.5 years and weighing 21.3 kg, had idiopathic paraphimosis with signs lasting 24 months. Examination upon presentation showed permanent penile protrusion, hyperaemia, and the penile protrusion measured 2.0 cm. The prepuce could easily be moved cranially to cover the protruded penis.

The dog underwent modified preputial elevation and cranial translation of the prepuce, with 4.0 cm of preputial translation, under general isoflurane anaesthesia. After surgery it was hospitalised for 2 days and received cryotherapy with ice packs. Re-examination 5 and 14 days after surgery found it clinically healthy with no signs of paraphimosis. The Figure 1 caption documents the surgical steps, ending in complete coverage of the penile exposure. No orchiectomy was performed at the time of surgery.

All dogs had a smooth recovery from anaesthesia and, per the abstract, recovered uneventfully from surgery. Table 1 records no short-term or long-term complications for this dog. Follow-up lasted 30 months and the outcome was graded excellent.

summary.text: Dog 4, an intact male mixed breed aged 0.5 years and weighing 3.7 kg, had idiopathic paraphimosis with signs lasting 1 month. Examination upon presentation showed permanent penile protrusion, hyperaemia, and the penile protrusion measured 3.0 cm. The prepuce could easily be moved cranially to cover the protruded penis.

The dog underwent modified preputial elevation and cranial translation of the prepuce, with 6.0 cm of preputial translation, under general isoflurane anaesthesia. After surgery it was hospitalised for 2 days and received cryotherapy with ice packs. Re-examination 5 and 14 days after surgery found it clinically healthy with no signs of paraphimosis. No orchiectomy was performed at the time of surgery.

Short-term complications were preputial oedema with mild penile protrusion of less than 0.5 cm, which resolved with ice packs then hot packs, and a 1.5 cm dehiscence on the right side of the inverted U incision, which was allowed to heal by second intention. No long-term complications were recorded. Follow-up lasted 18 months with an excellent outcome.

summary.text: Dog 5, a castrated male Yorkshire terrier aged 4.5 years and weighing 1.9 kg, had idiopathic paraphimosis with signs lasting 36 months. Examination upon presentation showed permanent penile protrusion, hyperaemia, and the penile protrusion measured 2.5 cm. The prepuce could easily be moved cranially to cover the protruded penis. The referring veterinarian had made a triangular full-thickness incision at the ventral prepuce to widen the orifice without success.

The dog underwent modified preputial elevation and cranial translation of the prepuce, with 5.0 cm of preputial translation, under general isoflurane anaesthesia. After surgery it was hospitalised for 2 days and received cryotherapy with ice packs. Re-examination 5 and 14 days after surgery found it clinically healthy with no signs of paraphimosis. The triangular defect at the ventral prepuce was closed in two layers.

Short-term complications were preputial oedema with mild penile protrusion, resolved with ice packs then hot packs; the wound was healed and oedema resolved 1 month after surgery. At re-examination 14 months after surgery a 0.5 cm intermittent protrusion without clinical significance was reported, which the Discussion calls a recurrence, and no revision surgery was deemed necessary. Table 1 grades the outcome Good, whereas the abstract says all dogs had an excellent outcome.
